c.v: In the factory function, the product varies and the caller chooses, by passing a value. In Factory Method, the product varies and a subclass chooses, by overriding, so the choice is fixed in the type of the object and the base class's workflow never learns which product it got. The factory function has one hierarchy, the controllers. Factory Method has two, the controllers and the scenarios, and every combination of workflow and product is a class.
You pass if the factory function returns the base by
and the Factory Method version puts the creation step behind a protected virtual function the base calls. Calling
's constructor is a fail, for the reason the failure cases section measures.

A factory is a function that builds an object in place of a constructor. Factory Method is one shape of it: a base class owns a multi-step workflow in an ordinary member function that calls a protected virtual step whose only job is to create the object the workflow uses; each subclass overrides that step to supply its own product. A simple factory function is the plainer alternative: one free function that takes an enumeration naming the product and returns it behind a

Both exist because a constructor cannot make this decision: it either produces the object or throws, so it cannot hand back a failure as a value, and it cannot return a type other than its own class, so it cannot read a value at run time and decide which of several products to build, the way reading a planner's kind from a parameter file needs.

A simple factory function puts that decision where the caller makes it: it passes an enumeration, and a switch returns the matching product, one hierarchy, the products, with no inheritance in the factory. Factory Method moves the decision into the type system instead: the algorithm is fixed in the base class, the creation step is pure virtual, and a subclass answers it by overriding, so the product is fixed the moment the subclass is chosen and the workflow never learns which one it got, needing two hierarchies, the products and the workflows, with every pairing its own class.

The costs are the class count and one trap. A workflow times four products is already several subclasses holding one line each, and each is a place a future change must repeat. Worse, calling the creation step from the base class's own constructor compiles without warning and never reaches the subclass, because during a constructor the dynamic type is still the base, so it silently builds the base's own idea of the product. Where a class does not truly own a multi-step workflow, handing the finished object in through the constructor instead avoids both problems.

You meet the simple factory function in nearly every ROS node that reads a kind from a parameter, and Factory Method wherever a base class genuinely owns the steps and only the object inside them changes, which is the interview question itself: saying which one chooses the product, and how.

subs.title: Factory Method versus simple factory versus registry

Four larger reasons follow, and each one is a thing a constructor cannot do.

items.v: A constructor cannot report failure with a value. It either produces the object or throws, because there is no object to hold a failure in (
puts it the other way round: a constructor that cannot build a valid object should throw). A function can return
A constructor cannot return a different type. A factory returns
and decides at run time whether the object behind it is a

A constructor cannot call a virtual function and reach the derived class, because during it the dynamic type is the class whose constructor is running, as the polymorphism topic showed. Core Guidelines
exists for this: use a factory function when you need virtual behaviour during initialisation.
A constructor always builds a new object. A factory can hand back a cached one, an object from a pool, or a value with no allocation at all.

c.v: Klaus Iglberger's Guideline 13 in C++ Software Design points out that you have been using factories all along:
is the one that decides to put the control block and the object in one allocation. The three shapes worth telling apart are these.
A simple factory function is a free function or a static member that takes a value and returns an object, usually a

to a base. There is one hierarchy, the products, and no inheritance at the factory itself. This is the shape ROS code wants nearly every time, because the choice arrives as a parameter and the set of products is known to the package that reads it.
Factory Method is a virtual creation step inside a workflow that a base class owns. The base's non-virtual function runs the algorithm and calls the protected virtual
; a subclass overrides that one step. The 1994 catalogue's summary is that the class defers deciding which type to build to its subclasses (

, the creational chapter). There are two hierarchies, the products and the creators, and the creator's type decides the product's type once and for all. The shape is Template Method with the varying step being an object creation, and it carries Template Method's cost with it: every pair of workflow and product is a class.
A registry is a table from a name to a creator function, filled at run time. It is the only one of the three that lets a package this one was never linked against add a product, which is what ROS 2's
is: a package declares a class in an XML manifest and registers it with
, and a node loads it by name from a parameter. The price is a table the whole process shares and anyone can change, which the failure cases section shows.
Pick by where the choice comes from and how open the set is.

items.v: The choice is a parameter and the set is closed: a simple factory function over an enumeration, with a separate step that turns the parameter's text into that enumeration and returns
. The worked example is this shape.
The set is open and other packages supply it: a registry, and pass it to whoever needs it rather than reaching for a global one.

A base class really owns a multi-step workflow and only one object inside it varies: Factory Method. If that is not the case, hand the object in instead, which is the dependency injection topic's constructor injection and Iglberger's Guideline 20, composition over inheritance.

c.v: One rule cuts across all three. Keep the step that can fail apart from the step that builds. Validation reads text and numbers and answers with a value; creation takes something already valid and cannot fail. A ROS 2 node that throws from its constructor produces no node at all, so the only place the reason can be printed is wherever

catches it, without the node's own logger and without the node name in the line. A node that reads a config and gets an error back can log it against its own logger and either carry on with a default or shut down deliberately.

This is the shape a node uses at start-up: five parameter files, two of them wrong, then a factory that builds the planner. It also counts the allocations, using the one piece of state the language forces to namespace scope.
